chunks: My father narrated (may God be pleased with him) said: Sa'd ibn Abdullah narrated from Yaqub ibn Yazid, from Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr, from more than one person, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

Saturday is for us, Sunday is for our followers, Monday is for our enemies, Tuesday is for the Banu Umayya, Wednesday is the day of drinking medicine, Thursday is for fulfilling needs, Friday is for cleanliness and perfuming, and it is the Eid of the Muslims and it is better than Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha, and the Day of Ghadir is the best of the Eids, and it is the eighteenth of Dhul-Hijjah and it was a Friday, and our Riser from the Ahl al-Bayt will emerge on a Friday, and the Resurrection will be on a Friday, and no deed on Friday is better than sending blessings upon Muhammad and his Household.

key_terms.أَهْلُ الْبَيْتِ: The People of the House (Ahl al-Bayt)
key_terms.الصَّلَاةِ عَلَى مُحَمَّدٍ وَآلِهِ: Sending blessings upon Muhammad and his Household

ai.seo_question: What is the significance of each day of the week and why is Friday considered the best day in Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This narration from Shaykh al-Saduq’s *Al-Khisal* reflects the Shia tradition of *Tajalliyat* (divine manifestations) on specific days, assigning spiritual or historical significance to each day of the week, with Friday (*Yawm al-Jum'a*) elevated as the preeminent day for Muslims. It uniquely identifies the Day of Ghadir (18th Dhu al-Hijjah) as the greatest Eid and links the emergence of the Qa'im and the Day of Resurrection to Friday, emphasizing the centrality of *Salat al-Muhammad* (blessings upon the Prophet and his Household) as the superior act of worship on this day. This underscores the Shia view of Friday not merely as a day of congregational prayer but as a cosmic day of divine favor and eschatological significance tied to the Ahl al-Bayt.
